prompt: A Cloud Run service deploys and passes its health check, then hangs on its first query to a database at 10.20.0.3. What is missing?
hint: Where does the instance run, and where is the database?

choices.text: A firewall rule allowing port 5432 from the internet
choices.why: Opening the database to the internet is the opposite of the fix, and the instance still has no private route.

choices.text: A route from the instance into the VPC
choices.why: Right. The instance runs on Google's network, which has no route into yours until the revision is given one.

choices.text: A larger instance size, because the query timed out
choices.why: The connection never opened; size has nothing to do with a missing route.

choices.text: The roles/run.invoker role on the database
choices.why: That role is about who may call a Cloud Run service, not about reaching a database.

prompt: Where is the VPC access of a Cloud Run service configured?
hint: Which part of a service can be split between two versions?

choices.text: On the project, for every service at once
choices.why: Each service decides, and within it each revision.

choices.text: On the VPC, by listing the services allowed in
choices.why: The VPC does not list Cloud Run services; the revision names the network.

choices.text: In the revision template, so each revision carries its own
choices.why: Right. A new revision can move from a connector to direct egress, and traffic can be split between them.

choices.text: In the container image, through an environment variable
choices.why: An environment variable can carry an address, not a route.

prompt: The orders service now reaches 10.20.0.3. What does that give it on the database?
hint: A private address is a route.

choices.text: Read access, because traffic from inside the VPC is trusted
choices.why: Being inside grants no database permission.

choices.text: Whatever its service account is allowed on the project
choices.why: Project roles do not log in to PostgreSQL by themselves.

choices.text: Full access, until a firewall rule says otherwise
choices.why: A firewall decides reachability, not database rights.

choices.text: Nothing yet: it still needs a database login
choices.why: Right. A private address is a route, not a permission: a database user or IAM authentication is still needed.

prompt: Match each mechanism to what it puts in the VPC.
hint: One puts the instance itself there.

pairs.right: An address for each instance, in a subnet you choose
A few small machines in a /28 that forward the traffic
A way out of the VPC to the internet from a reserved address

right_distractors: A copy of the database inside Google's network

prompt: Without VPC access, a connection from Cloud Run to a private address does not fail at once: it ___ out.
hint: What happens when nothing ever answers?

prompt: What does direct VPC egress add to the bill, apart from the traffic itself?
hint: Is anything running in between?

choices.text: A connector's e2-micro machines, at least two
choices.why: That is the connector's cost; direct egress has no machines.

choices.text: Nothing: no machines run in between
choices.why: Right. Each instance is in the subnet itself, so there is nothing to bill by the hour.

choices.text: A fee per subnet address, charged each hour
choices.why: Addresses in your subnet are not billed one by one.

choices.text: A Cloud NAT gateway, which it creates for you
choices.why: Nothing creates a NAT for you; it is needed only for ALL_TRAFFIC to the internet.

prompt: During a traffic burst, a service with direct egress stops adding instances and requests queue, while the service's own maximum is far away. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: What does every running instance hold?

choices.text: The connector reached max_instances and did not scale further
choices.why: With direct egress there is no connector.

choices.text: PRIVATE_RANGES_ONLY throttles new instances to protect the VPC
choices.why: The egress setting chooses routes; it limits nothing.

choices.text: The subnet has run out of free addresses
choices.why: Right. New instances cannot start without an address, and old ones release theirs only some time after stopping.

choices.text: The database refuses more than a fixed number of connections
choices.why: That would fail queries, not stop instances from starting.

prompt: Google reserves four addresses in every subnet. How many are left for instances in the /26 shop-run?
hint: A /26 has 2 to the power of 6 addresses.

prompt: terraform plan accepted network = "shop" and subnetwork = "shop-run". What has been checked?
hint: Who knows which subnets exist?

choices.text: Only that the block is shaped the way the provider expects
choices.why: Right. Cloud Run checks existence, region and free addresses when it creates the revision.

choices.text: That the subnet exists in southamerica-east1
choices.why: The plan asked nobody; the lab has no network at all.

choices.text: That the subnet has room for the maximum instance count
choices.why: Nothing in the plan counts addresses.

choices.text: That the database at 10.20.0.3 answers on port 5432
choices.why: The address is only an environment variable to Terraform.

prompt: In the revision template, the block that holds network_interfaces is called vpc____.
hint: The same block also holds egress.

prompt: A connector keeps min_instances = 2 of e2-micro, at 6.11 USD a month each. What is its floor for a year?
hint: Two machines, twelve months.

prompt: After a burst, a connector is still running its three instances at three in the morning. Why?
hint: It grows under load. What does it do afterwards?

choices.text: min_instances was raised to 3 by the burst
choices.why: Nothing rewrites min_instances.

choices.text: Cloud Run keeps idle instances warm through the connector
choices.why: Cloud Run's idle instances do not hold connector machines up.

choices.text: A connector scales out under load and does not scale back in by itself
choices.why: Right. It can stay at its maximum until somebody notices, and it is billed all the while.

choices.text: The /28 range needs three machines to stay routable
choices.why: The range is reserved either way; machines do not keep it routable.

prompt: A revision has both connector = google_vpc_access_connector.shop.id and a network_interfaces block, and terraform plan is clean. What does that clean plan mean?
hint: What does Terraform know about the connector's id before it exists?

choices.text: That Cloud Run accepts both mechanisms on one revision
choices.why: It does not; with a literal id the provider itself refuses the pair.

choices.text: That the network_interfaces block is ignored when a connector is set
choices.why: Nothing ignores it; the rule is that they conflict.

choices.text: Only that the rule could not be checked yet
choices.why: Right. The refusal would come from Cloud Run when the revision is created.

choices.text: That the connector will be created first and then removed
choices.why: The plan says 2 to add and nothing about removal.

prompt: In which of these situations is a connector still a reasonable choice? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of address space and of what was built around the connector.

choices.text: A firewall rule admits 10.8.0.0/28 and nothing else
choices.why: Right; the fixed range is what the network was built around.

choices.text: The network team will give a /28 and no room for a larger subnet
choices.why: Right; direct egress needs addresses for every instance.

choices.text: The service must not pay anything at night
choices.why: A connector has a floor billed all night.

choices.text: The service is new and the subnet is empty
choices.why: That is the case direct egress is recommended for.

prompt: A connector's ip_cidr_range is a /___ of its own, sixteen addresses.
hint: Two to the power of four is sixteen.

prompt: Which setting decides who may send requests to a Cloud Run service?
hint: One is about callers, the other about the service's own connections.

choices.text: Egress, on the vpc_access block
choices.why: Egress is where outbound connections go.

choices.text: The subnet the instances take addresses from
choices.why: That is part of egress.

choices.text: Ingress, set on the service as a whole
choices.why: Right; IAM's invoker role is the identity half of the same question.

choices.text: The connector's machine type
choices.why: A connector carries outbound traffic only.

prompt: orders is set to INGRESS_TRAFFIC_INTERNAL_ONLY. Calls from web, another Cloud Run service with no VPC access, are refused. Why?
hint: How does a call from web leave web?

choices.text: web lacks roles/run.invoker on orders
choices.why: That would be an identity refusal; here the network setting refuses first.

choices.text: Its calls do not leave through the VPC
choices.why: Right. They arrive over Google's network, so they are not internal; give web direct egress and they arrive from inside.

choices.text: Two Cloud Run services can never call each other
choices.why: They can; the call has to count as internal.

choices.text: INGRESS_TRAFFIC_INTERNAL_ONLY accepts only Compute Engine callers
choices.why: It accepts anything arriving from the VPC, including Cloud Run with egress.

prompt: A partner's API admits one fixed IP address. What does the calling service need?
hint: Where does traffic go with ALL_TRAFFIC, and how does it leave?

choices.text: PRIVATE_RANGES_ONLY, so its public calls keep one address
choices.why: With that value public calls leave from Cloud Run's shared addresses.

choices.text: A connector, whose machines keep their public addresses
choices.why: A connector forwards into the VPC; the way out is still the VPC's.

choices.text: INGRESS_TRAFFIC_INTERNAL_LOAD_BALANCER with a static address
choices.why: Ingress is about calls in, not calls out.

choices.text: ALL_TRAFFIC into the VPC, and Cloud NAT with a reserved address
choices.why: Right. Every outbound request then leaves from that address.

prompt: A revision switches from PRIVATE_RANGES_ONLY to ALL_TRAFFIC in a VPC with no Cloud NAT. What breaks?
hint: Where does a call to a public address go now?

choices.text: The private database, because public and private now share one route
choices.why: Private addresses are reached exactly as before.

choices.text: Calls to the internet, which now follow the VPC's routes and find no way out
choices.why: Right. ALL_TRAFFIC sends everything into the VPC; the internet needs NAT from there.

choices.text: Incoming requests, because ingress follows egress
choices.why: Changing egress never changes ingress.

choices.text: Nothing: Cloud Run adds a NAT automatically
choices.why: Nothing adds a NAT for you.

prompt: Ingress is a network check; the identity check on who may call a service is IAM's roles/run.___ role.
hint: The role that lets a caller invoke.

prompt: Put the steps of giving the orders service access to its private database in a sensible order.
hint: The address space comes before anything uses it.
items: Set aside a subnet for Cloud Run, sized for the maximum instances
Add vpc_access with network_interfaces to the revision template
Deploy the new revision with egress PRIVATE_RANGES_ONLY
Give the service a database user or IAM authentication
trap: The database identity comes last only in the sense that the route must exist first; skipping it leaves a reachable database that refuses every login.

prompt: A connector with min_instances = 2 and max_instances = 5 of e2-micro (6.11 USD a month each) got stuck at its maximum after a burst. How much more a month does it cost than at its floor?
hint: Three extra machines.

prompt: The shop locks orders to INGRESS_TRAFFIC_INTERNAL_ONLY and keeps roles/run.invoker for web only. Which single change would let an attacker on the internet call orders?
hint: Both checks have to fail.

choices.text: Setting the ingress of orders to INGRESS_TRAFFIC_ALL
choices.why: The attacker still lacks the invoker role, so IAM refuses.

choices.text: Granting roles/run.invoker on orders to allUsers
choices.why: Ingress still refuses traffic from the internet.

choices.text: Switching the egress of orders to ALL_TRAFFIC everywhere
choices.why: Egress never changes who may call in.

choices.text: No single one of these; it takes both of the first two
choices.why: Right. Network and identity are separate checks, and each holds on its own.

prompt: Which of these did the lab actually check for lesson 12's Terraform files? Choose all that apply.
hint: Everything that runs is on your laptop.

choices.text: That ingress and egress values are among the accepted ones
choices.why: Right; the provider refused INTERNAL and PRIVATE_ONLY.

choices.text: That a literal connector id conflicts with network_interfaces
choices.why: Right; both blocks were named in both errors.

choices.text: That the subnet shop-run has free addresses
choices.why: Only Cloud Run can know that.

choices.text: That the database answers from inside the VPC
choices.why: No database and no VPC exist in the lab.
